claim: Bacteria use diverse immunity mechanisms to defend themselves against their viral predators, bacteriophages.
source: Bacteria use diverse immunity mechanisms to defend themselves against their viral predators, bacteriophages.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial defense mechanisms.

claim: Phages can acquire counter-defense systems.
source: In turn, phages can acquire counter-defense systems, but it remains unclear how such mechanisms arise and what factors constrain viral evolution.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of phage-bacteria interactions.

claim: T4 phage was experimentally evolved to overcome a phage-defensive toxin-antitoxin system, toxIN, in Escherichia coli.
source: Here, we experimentally evolved T4 phage to overcome a phage-defensive toxin-antitoxin system, toxIN, in Escherichia coli.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: T4 rapidly acquires segmental amplifications of tifA through recombination.
source: Through recombination, T4 rapidly acquires segmental amplifications of a previously uncharacterized gene, now named tifA, encoding an inhibitor of the toxin, ToxN.
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data showing increased read coverage at the tifA locus.

claim: tifA encodes an inhibitor of the toxin ToxN.
source: Through recombination, T4 rapidly acquires segmental amplifications of a previously uncharacterized gene, now named tifA, encoding an inhibitor of the toxin, ToxN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that tifA expression allows T4 to overcome toxIN-mediated defense.

claim: Segmental amplifications of tifA drive large deletions elsewhere in T4's genome to maintain a genome size compatible with capsid packaging.
source: These amplifications subsequently drive large deletions elsewhere in T4's genome to maintain a genome size compatible with capsid packaging.
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data showing deletions in evolved clones and the correlation between amplification size and deletion size.

claim: The deleted regions in evolved T4 include accessory genes that help T4 overcome defense systems in alternative hosts.
source: The deleted regions include accessory genes that help T4 overcome defense systems in alternative hosts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that evolved clones lost the ability to infect certain E. coli strains.

claim: The emergence of one counter-defense mechanism can lead to loss of other such mechanisms, thereby constraining host range.
source: Thus, our results reveal a trade-off in viral evolution; the emergence of one counter-defense mechanism can lead to loss of other such mechanisms, thereby constraining host range.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that evolved phages gained the ability to infect toxIN-containing hosts but lost the ability to infect other E. coli strains.

claim: The accessory genomes of viruses reflect the integrated evolutionary history of the hosts they infected.
source: We propose that the accessory genomes of viruses reflect the integrated evolutionary history of the hosts they infected.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: Bacteria have evolved a diverse arsenal of anti-phage defense systems.
source: Bacteria face the frequent threat of phage predation and have consequently evolved a diverse arsenal of anti-phage defense systems (Bernheim and Sorek, 2020; Tal and Sorek, 2022; Wein and Sorek, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bacterial defense systems have driven the selection of counter-defense mechanisms in phage.
source: These defense systems have, in turn, driven the selection of counter-defense mechanisms in phage, underscoring the intense arms race between phages and their bacterial hosts (Samson et al., 2013; Hampton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There are several well-characterized examples of anti-restriction modification (RM) and anti-CRISPR proteins.
source: There are several well-characterized examples of anti-restriction modification (RM) and anti-CRISPR proteins (Stanley and Maxwell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems are an emerging class of potent phage defense genes.
source: An emerging class of potent phage defense genes are toxin–antitoxin (TA) systems, which typically comprise a protein toxin that is directly neutralized by its cognate antitoxin (Harms et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: For defensive TA systems, phage infection activates or triggers the release of the toxin, which can then block phage development.
source: For defensive TA systems, phage infection activates or triggers the release of the toxin, which can then block phage development (Guegler and Laub, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: T4 encodes nearly 300 proteins, only 62 of which are required to produce a new virion in common laboratory conditions.
source: For instance, T4 encodes nearly 300 proteins, only 62 of which are required to produce a new virion in common laboratory conditions (Miller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The T4 gene dmd encodes a direct inhibitor of the RnlA toxin from the Escherichia coli K12 type II TA system RnlAB.
source: The T4 gene dmd encodes a direct inhibitor of the RnlA toxin from the Escherichia coli K12 type II TA system RnlAB (Otsuka and Yonesaki, 2012; Wan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: T-even phages including T4 encode an inhibitor (AdfA, encoded by gene 61.2 in T4) of DarT toxins.
source: More recently, T-even phages including T4 were shown to encode an inhibitor (AdfA, encoded by gene 61.2 in T4) of DarT toxins (LeRoux et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: T4 is restricted by +toxIN E. coli.
source: (A) T4 is restricted by +toxIN E. coli. Serial dilution plaquing assay of T4 spotted on -toxIN and +toxIN cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with plaquing assays.

claim: Phage that could form plaques on lawns of +toxIN cells arose after five rounds of evolution.
source: For one of the populations (evo 3), phage that could form plaques on lawns of +toxIN cells arose after five rounds of evolution, an estimated 5–15 infection generations.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during the evolution experiment.

claim: Evolved phages plaque as efficiently on +toxIN cells as on the control strain -toxIN.
source: From this population, we isolated phages from four individual plaques on +toxIN lawns and confirmed that these evolved phages plaque as efficiently on +toxIN cells as on the control strain -toxIN (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with plaquing assays.

claim: Genome sequencing revealed increased read coverage of a two-gene locus (dmd and 61.4) in the genome of each evolved clone.
source: However, our sequencing revealed increased read coverage of a two-gene locus in the genome of each evolved clone (Figure 1D). This locus consists of two genes, dmd (61.5) and 61.4, driven by an early T4 promoter (Liebig and Rüger, 1989; Miller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The increased read coverage of the dmd-tifA locus indicates a local, segmental amplification of this locus.
source: PCR using primers flanking this locus produced a ladder of products, indicating a segmental amplification generating tandem repeats (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The ability of toxIN to inhibit T4 infection was completely lost following induction of tifA.
source: The ability of toxIN to inhibit T4 infection was completely lost following induction of tifA, suggesting that this gene was sufficient to prevent ToxN-mediated defense.
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Overexpressing dmd did not allow T4 to replicate in the presence of toxIN.
source: Overexpressing dmd did not allow T4 to replicate in the presence of toxIN, indicating that this gene did not contribute to escape, but was likely included in the segmental amplification as the promoter for tifA lies upstream of dmd (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Co-induction of tifA was sufficient to partially rescue toxicity of ToxN in uninfected cells.
source: Co-induction of tifA was sufficient to partially rescue this toxicity, on both solid media and in culture (Figure 2B,C), indicating that tifA is a T4-encoded antitoxin for ToxN.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: tifA encodes a protein antitoxin rather than an RNA antitoxin.
source: Expressing a version of tifA in which the start codon was deleted (tifA ΔATG) could no longer restore T4 infection of cells harboring toxIN, suggesting that tifA must be translated to function.
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A recoded variant of tifA that has a different mRNA sequence but produces the same protein sequence could still restore T4 infection of +toxIN cells.
source: Additionally, we found that a recoded variant of tifA that has a different mRNA sequence (55 of 258 nucleotides changed) but produces the same protein sequence could still restore T4 infection of +toxIN cells, indicating that the protein product of tifA was sufficient for ToxN inhibition.
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TifA interacts with ToxN in vivo.
source: Western blotting with an anti-FLAG antibody confirmed that TifA was present, as expected, and blotting with an anti-His6 antibody demonstrated that ToxN was also recovered (Figure 2E). These results suggest that TifA interacts with ToxN, either directly or indirectly, in vivo.
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Native tifA expression is sufficient to overcome ToxN produced from the chromosome.
source: These results suggest that native tifA expression is sufficient to overcome ToxN produced from the chromosome and that the segmental amplification that arose during our evolution experiments reflects a pressure to overcome the stronger expression of plasmid-borne toxIN.
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Homologs of tifA are found adjacent to dmd homologs in the genomes of the coliphage T2, T6, and RB69.
source: Homologs of tifA are found adjacent to dmd homologs in the genomes of the coliphage T2, T6, and RB69, all of which are closely related to T4 (Figure 3A), and in other types of phages that infect a diverse set of bacterial hosts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on genome comparisons shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Plasmid-borne toxIN strongly protects E. coli against T2, T4, and T6 infection, but offers substantially less protection against RB69.
source: Interestingly, plasmid-borne toxIN strongly protects E. coli against T2, T4, and T6 infection, but offers substantially less protection against RB69, as measured by plaquing efficiency and cell death in shaking cultures (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays and growth curves shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: All TifA homologs from T2, T4, T6, and RB69 can rescue cells from ToxN-mediated toxicity to some extent.
source: Finally, we expressed each tifA homolog in uninfected cells ectopically producing ToxN and found that all the TifA homologs rescued cells from ToxN-mediated toxicity to some extent (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ToxIN-resistant phages emerged at a different round in each population.
source: ToxIN-resistant phages emerged at a different round in each population, but with comparable levels of resistance stabilizing after 25 rounds (Figure 4A ,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on serial dilution plaquing assays shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Each sequenced genome from evolved populations had an amplification of the dmd-tifA locus.
source: However, as with the first clones sequenced (Figure 1D), each of these sequenced genomes had an amplification of the dmd-tifA locus, as manifested by an approximately tenfold increase in read counts in this region (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The precise boundaries of the segmental amplification differed in each evolved population.
source: The precise boundaries of the segmental amplification differed in each evolved population. This finding indicates that the same adaptive solution, the amplification of the dmd-tifA locus, occurred independently in each evolved population.
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing and PCR data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The boundaries of each segmental amplification coincided with unique, short (typically 6–10 bp) regions of microhomology that normally flank the dmd-tifA locus.
source: Sanger sequencing of the PCR products revealed that the boundaries of each segmental amplification coincided with unique, short (typically 6–10 bp) regions of microhomology that normally flank the dmd-tifA locus (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on Sanger sequencing of PCR products.

claim: The segmental amplifications observed likely arose through homologous recombination between regions of microhomology.
source: Thus, the segmental amplifications observed likely arose through homologous recombination between these regions of microhomology, as also seen previously in T4 (Kumagai et al., 1993; Mosig, 1987; Wu et al., 1991; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Each evolved clone of T4 had large deletions elsewhere in its genome.
source: Strikingly, in addition to an amplification of the dmd-tifA locus, each evolved clone of T4 also had large deletions elsewhere in its genome (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Individual deletions were different in each clone and ranged from 0.7 to 6 kb in length, for a total of 5–11 kb lost in each genome.
source: Individual deletions were different in each clone and ranged from 0.7 to 6 kb in length, for a total of 5–11 kb lost in each genome (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The size of the deleted region in each evolved clone was roughly proportional to the size of the segmental amplification.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the size of the deleted region in each evolved clone was roughly proportional to the size of the segmental amplification, as estimated from the increased read coverage across the dmd-tifA region (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: None of the 62 genes that are essential for producing new virions during infection of E. coli in rich media at 37°C were included in the deletions identified in evolved clones.
source: None of the 62 genes that are essential for producing new virions during infection of E. coli in rich media at 37°C (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) were included in the deletions identified in our evolved clones (Miller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on comparison of deletion regions with known essential genes.

claim: The T4 clones that have deletions spanning rII lost the ability to replicate on a λ-lysogen of MG1655.
source: As predicted, the T4 clones that have deletions spanning rII lost the ability to replicate on a λ-lysogen of MG1655 (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Expressing rIIA and rIIB from plasmids in a MG1655 λ-lysogen partially restored the infectivity of an evolved T4 clone.
source: Expressing rIIA and rIIB from plasmids in a MG1655 λ-lysogen partially restored the infectivity of an evolved T4 clone, confirming the causal nature of the rII deletion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Clones from populations 1, 2, 3, and 5 failed to infect ECOR17.
source: Clones from populations 1, 2, 3, and 5 (evo 1, 2, 3, and 5) failed to infect ECOR17 and clones from populations 1 and 3 (evo 1 and 3) failed to infect ECOR71 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The only gene lost in common across clones in evo 1, 2, and 5 was ipIII.
source: The only gene lost in common across clones in evo 1, 2, and 5 was ipIII, implying that it enables T4 to infect ECOR17 (Figure 5B and Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of deletion regions across evolved clones.

claim: Providing ipIIIT4 on a plasmid in ECOR17 restored the ability of clones from evo 2 and 5 to infect this host.
source: Indeed, providing ipIIIT4 on a plasmid in ECOR17 restored the ability of clones from evo 2 and 5 to infect this host (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A disruption of dsr1 in ECOR17 restored infection by the evo 3 clone.
source: For this clone, a disruption of dsr1 in ECOR17 restored infection (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Expressing the T4 early gene nrdC.5 under an inducible promoter restored infectivity of the evo 3 clone on MG1655 carrying dsr1.
source: Expressing the uncharacterized T4 early gene nrdC.5 under an inducible promoter restored infectivity of the evo 3 clone on MG1655 carrying dsr1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TifA is analogous to the co-operonic gene dmd, which encodes a direct inhibitor of RnlA.
source: TifA is analogous to the co-operonic gene dmd, which encodes a direct inhibitor of RnlA, the toxin of the rnlAB system in E. coli.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about dmd function.

claim: The nearby and conserved gene 61.2 (now adfA) was recently found to overcome the type IV TA system darTG.
source: Additionally, the nearby and conserved gene 61.2 (now adfA) was recently found to overcome the type IV TA system darTG (LeRoux et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: This region of the T4 genome may be an anti-TA island.
source: Thus, this region of the T4 genome may be an anti-TA island, similar to the anti-RM and anti-CRISPR islands found in other phages (Pinilla-Redondo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of multiple anti-TA genes in this region and supported by a citation.

claim: T4 evolved to overcome toxIN by amplifying dmd-tifA, likely via recombination between short homologous sequences that flank this locus.
source: T4 evolved to overcome toxIN by amplifying dmd-tifA, likely via recombination between short homologous sequences that flank this locus.
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data showing amplifications with boundaries at regions of microhomology.

claim: T4 can undergo large genomic changes through recombination between short regions of homology, leading to loss of the intervening region.
source: Our work also indicates that T4 can undergo large genomic changes through recombination between short regions of homology, leading to loss of the intervening region (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data showing deletions with boundaries at regions of microhomology.

claim: Genome packaging in T4 proceeds via a headful mechanism.
source: Genome packaging in T4 proceeds via a headful mechanism (Rao and Black, 2005), so any substantial gain in DNA must be offset by comparably sized losses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The gains in genetic material resulting from amplification of dmd-tifA likely necessitated the loss of other, nonessential DNA to maintain a genome that could be fully packaged into the head.
source: Thus, the gains in genetic material resulting from amplification of dmd-tifA likely necessitated the loss of other, nonessential DNA to maintain a genome that could be fully packaged into the head.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that amplification size correlates with deletion size.

claim: The accessory genomes of phages likely include a broad range of anti-defense genes that profoundly influence their host ranges.
source: The accessory genomes of phages likely include a broad range of anti-defense genes that profoundly influence their host ranges.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings that deletion of accessory genes compromised infection of certain hosts.

claim: If selection to infect a host and overcome its defense systems is not maintained, the corresponding anti-defense genes can be lost following pressure to infect new and different hosts.
source: As our experimental evolution demonstrates, if selection to infect a host and overcome its defense systems is not maintained, the corresponding anti-defense genes, which are not essential for phage replication, can be lost following pressure to infect new and different hosts (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the experimental evolution results showing loss of anti-defense genes.

claim: The characterization of evolved T4 isolates indicated that IPIII likely antagonizes a novel, as-yet unknown defense system in ECOR17.
source: In addition to finding TifA as a novel inhibitor of ToxN, the characterization of our evolved T4 isolates indicated that IPIII likely antagonizes a novel, as-yet unknown defense system in ECOR17.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IPIII is required for infection of ECOR17 but the target defense system is unknown.

claim: A homolog of the recently identified Dsr1 system in ECOR17 can be counteracted by the nonessential gene nrdC.5 in wild-type T4.
source: Additionally, we discovered a homolog of the recently identified Dsr1 system in ECOR17 that can be counteracted by the nonessential gene nrdC.5 in wild-type T4.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing that nrdC.5 expression restores infection in the presence of dsr1.

claim: The T4 genome is packaged by a headful mechanism in which 172 kb from a genomic concatemer is inserted into a pro-head.
source: The T4 genome is packaged by a headful mechanism in which 172 kb from a genomic concatemer is inserted into a pro-head. The inserted DNA represents 102% of the T4 genome (168 kb), with ~3.3 kb of terminal redundancy (Grossi et al., 1983; Kim and Davidson, 1974; Rao and Black, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The segmental amplifications that arose following selection on +toxIN cells likely required the genome to contract elsewhere to ensure stable packaging and inheritance of the genome.
source: To ensure stable packaging and inheritance of the genome, the segmental amplifications that arose following selection on +toxIN cells likely required the genome to contract elsewhere.
evidence: This is inferred from the headful packaging mechanism and the observation of compensatory deletions.

claim: The RexAB system of λ allows it to exclude T4 rII mutants by a mechanism that remains poorly characterized.
source: The RexAB system of λ allows it to exclude T4 rII mutants by a mechanism that remains poorly characterized (Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: IPI inhibits the restriction-modification system gmrSD.
source: IPI inhibits the restriction-modification system gmrSD (Bair and Black, 2007), but the function of the other internal proteins is not known.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Dsr1 contains a Sirtuin domain and likely blocks phage replication by disrupting cytoplasmic NAD+ levels.
source: Dsr1 contains a Sirtuin domain and likely blocks phage replication by disrupting cytoplasmic NAD+ levels (Garb et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: T-even phages encode a set of proteins called internal proteins that contain a sequence motif that drives packaging into mature virions such that the proteins are injected into a host with the phage genome.
source: T-even phages encode a set of proteins – including IPIII – called internal proteins: they contain a sequence motif that drives packaging into mature virions such that the proteins are injected into a host with the phage genome (Kutter et al., 1995; Leiman et al., 2003; Mullaney and Black, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IPIII functions in the cytoplasm of ECOR17 to enable T4 replication.
source: We also found that having the host cells express a variant of IPIII lacking the capsid-targeting sequence (ipIIIT4ΔCTS) restored infectivity of clones from evo 2 and 5, indicating that IPIII functions in the cytoplasm of ECOR17 to enable T4 replication (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The T4 population titer remained at 105–106 pfu/µL throughout the evolution protocol.
source: Throughout the evolution protocol, the T4 population titer remained at 105–106 pfu/µL, with an estimated 1–3 phage infection generations occurring in wells from high to low MOI within a single round of evolution (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during the evolution experiment.

claim: An estimated 1–3 phage infection generations occurred in wells from high to low MOI within a single round of evolution.
source: Throughout the evolution protocol, the T4 population titer remained at 105–106 pfu/µL, with an estimated 1–3 phage infection generations occurring in wells from high to low MOI within a single round of evolution (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on calculations described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: toxIN was previously identified and characterized as a type III TA system from an environmental isolate of E. coli that strongly protects E. coli MG1655 against T4 infection.
source: We previously identified and characterized toxINEc (hereafter toxIN for simplicity), a type III TA system from an environmental isolate of E. coli that strongly protects E. coli MG1655 against T4 infection (Figure 1A; Guegler and Laub, 2021).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: The Appelmans protocol was originally developed in phage therapy to evolve phage to replicate on resistant pathogenic hosts.
source: To evolve T4 to overcome toxIN, we adapted the Appelmans protocol originally developed in phage therapy to evolve phage to replicate on resistant pathogenic hosts (Appelmans, 1921; Burrowes et al., 2019; Mapes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The native antitoxin toxI is an untranslated RNA that binds and neutralizes ToxN.
source: Given that the native antitoxin toxI is an untranslated RNA that binds and neutralizes ToxN, we sought to determine whether tifA encodes a protein or an RNA antitoxin of ToxN (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the toxIN system.

claim: TifA homologs share a common architecture, with a central region containing a cluster of positively charged residues.
source: TifA homologs share a common architecture, with a central region containing a cluster of positively charged residues (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The T2, T4, and T6 TifA homologs are nearly identical to one another.
source: Although the T2, T4, and T6 homologs are nearly identical to one another, RB69 TifA is more divergent (56% identity) and lacks the C-terminal extension shared by the other three (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RB69 TifA is more divergent (56% identity) and lacks the C-terminal extension shared by T2, T4, and T6 TifA.
source: Although the T2, T4, and T6 homologs are nearly identical to one another, RB69 TifA is more divergent (56% identity) and lacks the C-terminal extension shared by the other three (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RB69 TifA may be a more potent inhibitor of ToxN.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that the more divergent TifA from RB69 may be a more potent inhibitor of ToxN.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RB69 is less affected by toxIN than other T-even phages.

claim: RB69 TifA produced the clearest plaques when overexpressed in +toxIN cells infected with T4.
source: Overexpressing any of the four TifA variants allowed T4 to form plaques on +toxIN lawns (Figure 3D), with cells producing RB69 TifA producing the clearest plaques.
evidence: This is based on plaquing assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Similar recombination events between short (2–10 bp) regions of homology in T4 have been seen previously in studies of the rII locus.
source: Similar recombination events between short (2–10 bp) regions of homology in T4 have been seen previously in studies of the rII locus (Kumagai et al., 1993), genes 16–18 (Wu et al., 1991), and escape from CRISPR-Cas defense (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A similar pattern of gene amplification in the 16–18 region of T4 followed by deletion of the gene alt was previously reported.
source: A similar pattern of gene amplification in the 16–18 region of T4 followed by deletion of the gene alt was previously reported (Wu et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Gene amplification is a major source of evolutionary innovation.
source: Gene amplification is a major source of evolutionary innovation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria frequently arises through gene amplification.
source: For instance, antibiotic resistance in bacteria frequently arises through gene amplification.
evidence: This is established knowledge in microbiology.

claim: Spontaneous tandem duplications arise frequently in bacterial genomes and can be present in as much as 3% of a population.
source: Seminal studies of Salmonella demonstrated that spontaneous tandem duplications arise frequently in bacterial genomes and can be present in as much as 3% of a population (Anderson and Roth, 1981; Anderson and Roth, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Selection for poxviruses that can overcome the host restriction factor protein kinase R revealed an initial segmental amplification of the anti-host factor K3L, followed by subsequent acquisition of a beneficial point mutation in one copy K3L and subsequent loss of additional copies of the gene.
source: Similarly, a selection for poxviruses that can overcome the host restriction factor protein kinase R revealed an initial segmental amplification of the anti-host factor K3L, followed by subsequent acquisition of a beneficial point mutation in one copy K3L and subsequent loss of additional copies of the gene (Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The entire T4 ancestor population likely contains a single copy of the dmd-tifA locus, which is insufficient to overcome plasmid-borne toxIN.
source: In the case of tifA, the entire T4 ancestor population likely contains a single copy of the dmd-tifA locus, which is insufficient to overcome plasmid-borne toxIN.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that wild-type T4 cannot infect +toxIN cells.

claim: The segmental amplifications via recombination arose within several rounds in each of the replicate populations.
source: However, the recombination events leading to these amplifications arose within several rounds in each of our replicate populations, indicating that this is a readily available pathway to overcoming toxIN.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during the evolution experiment.

claim: Point mutations in tifA that improve its inhibition of ToxN were not observed early on.
source: We did not observe point mutations in tifA early on that improve its inhibition of ToxN, likely because segmental amplifications via recombination arise more frequently.
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data from evolved clones.

claim: Beneficial point mutations arising after the segmental amplifications, leading to subsequent collapse of the amplification, were not observed.
source: We also did not observe beneficial point mutations arising after the segmental amplifications, leading to subsequent collapse of the amplification, as with protein kinase R.
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data from evolved clones.
